(iii) It lacks guidelines for the conduct of its exercise thus enabling it to be used and grossly abused by the Government and the Police (Sub-Inspector and Inspectors who are entrusted to record the first information report and investigate the case) to "Pick and Choose" between persons similarly situated and normally liable to be prosecuted under the ordinary law of the land i.e. the Penal Code and the Criminal Procedure Code, briefly CrPC, by arbitrarily and maliciously exposing them to the harsher Provisions of the PSA. 

 (x) It lacks the procedural safeguard and fairness of trial as section 18 of the PSA provides that the tribunal shall try cases summarily in accordance with section 264 of the CrPC: that chapter XX of the Said Code shall as far as practicable be followed and that instead of recording the testimony of the witnesses in full only the substance of the same shall be recorded. Chapter XX of the CrPC speaks of the trial of summons cases by Magistrates while Chapter XXI speaks of trial of warrant cases by Magistrates. The difference and distinction that once existed between summons procedure and warrant procedure have long been done away with. Now there is only one procedure i.e. warrant procedure. Whereas section 264 which comes under Chapter XXII of the CrPC. (of Summary trial) provides that in every case tried summarily by a Magistrate, such Magistrate shall before passing sentence record judgment embodying the substance of the evidence and that such judgment sjiall be the only record in cases coming within this section. While section 260 of the CrPC provides that any first class Magistrate specially empowered by the government if he thinks fit may try in a summary way all or any of the following offences: 

 Professor Wade in his Administrative Law (sixth edition) in dealing with procedural justice said "Procedure is not a matter of secondary importance. As governmental powers continually grow more drastic, it is only by procedural fairness that they are rendered tolerable. The legislation which controls the use of land, for example, contains a large element of expropriation without compensation, which is for the most part accepted without pubic complaint. But if there is the least suggestion that planning appeal has been handled unfairly, public complaint is loud and widespread. Mr Frankfurter, a Judge of the United States Supreme Court, said; in the case of Shaughnessy vs United States 345 US (1943) "procedural fairness and regularity are of the indispensable essence of liberty. Severe substantive laws can be endured if they are fairly and impartially applied. He went on to say that it might be preferable to live under Russian Law applied by common law procedures than under the common law enforced by Russian Procedures. One of his colleagues said "The history of liberty has largely been the history of the observance of procedural safeguards." 

 (xiii) The extract/Summary of the Bill (PSA) was presented to the President for his recommendation to be introduced into the Parliament as a Bill involving expenditure of public moneys and not as a money Bill as required under Article 82 of the Constitution. And though the President recommended the same as a Bill involving expenditure of public moneys and not as a Money Bill, the Home Minister introduced the Bill into the House telling the legislature that it was recommended by the President as a Money Bill. This is a prevarication and travesty of truth, which is evident from Annexure "5" and "6" respectively of the affidavit-in-opposition of respondent No. 1 (Government). 

 2. Upon these assertions all the above Rules were issued on different dates calling upon the respondents (mainly the Government of Bangladesh) to show cause, why the PSA should not be declared to be void being ultra vires the fundamental rights guaranteed by Articles 27, 31, 32, and 35 of the Constitution and for violation of Articles 7, 26(2), 65(1), 81(1), 80(3), 101, 109 and 116A of the Constitution. 

 3. The PSA is comprised of 25 sections. And of those 25 sections the following are the Penal sections i.e. section 4 hijacking, 5 extortion or collection of subscription, 6 interference with tender, 7 causing damage and destruction to cars and properties, 8 obstruction to the plying of vehicles, 9 demand and realisation of ransom, 10 creating of panic, 11 filing of false cases and section 12 is abetment of offence. The rest of the sections deal with the powers, functions and jurisdiction of the Tribunal, Appeal and the Procedure as to bail and trial while section 25 (the last section) empowers the government to make rules which however was never made for reasons best known to the government. Certain amendments however were subsequently made in respect of sections 4/14/16/18 and 23 of the Act. 

 11. It is submitted that the PSA was not a Money Bill under Article 81(1) of the Constitution. The Government though asserted in their Affidavit-in-Opposition in Paragraph 7 (Seven) in Writ Petition No. 4430 of 2000 that the PSA was a Money Bill and was passed by the Parliament, certificated by the Speaker and assented to by the President as such because it was a Money Bill under Article 81(1)(d) of the Constitution. What is a money bill has been defined in Article 81(1) of the Constitution which runs as follows: 

 (b) the borrowing of money or the giving of any guarantee by the Government, or the amendment of any law relating to the financial obligations of the Government; 

 (e) the receipt of moneys on account of the Consolidated Fund or the Public Account of the Republic, or the custody or issue of such moneys, or the audit of the accounts of the Government; 

 (d) all debt charges for which the Government is liable, including interest, sinking fund charges, the repayment of amortisation of capital, and other expenditure in connection with the raising of loans and the service and redemption of debt; 

 13. In the case of Dira Dockyard and Engineers Ltd and others vs Shilpa Rin Sangstha and others 39 DLR (AD) 59 it was held that when the word "means" is used (in Article 81 of the Constitution the word means has been used in defining Money Bill saying "Money Bill" means:) in any clause or section it puts a limit, nothing more being in contemplation; but if the word "includes" is used it means something more than what is in terms specified. The use of the word "includes" does not exclude other possible meanings besides that have been expressly mentioned in the clause" and hence the definition of Money Bill is exhaustive. To counter this hurdle, the learned Attorney-General Mr Mahmudul Islam, argued that many such or similar Bills were passed and assented to by the President as Money Bills in the past by various governments and as such it has become a parliamentary practice. This was answered to by Mr Syed Ishtiaq Ahmed saying "such illegal and unconstitutional practice or precedent cannot be used as a justification for the present Bill being described as a Money Bill when it does not answer the description of Article 81(1) of the Constitution. I find tremendous force and substance in this argument and do accept it. There can be no estoppel against a statute and more so against the supreme law of the land which is the solemn expression of the will of the people i.e. the Constitution. 

 22. The learned Attorney-General disputes this proposition stating that the concept of colourable legislation is relatable only to a Federal System of Government where the Federal and Provincial legislatures encroach upon one another's domain in law making. Mr Ishtiaq Ahmed submits that this is not the universal rule. It may occur and did occur in this country and cited the case of Kudrat-e-Elahi Panir vs Bangladesh 44 DLR (AD) 319. In that case the Local Government (Upazila Parishad and Upazila Re-organisation) (Repeal) Ordinance, 1991 was challenged. By that Ordinance Upazila Parishads were abolished but the rights, powers, authorities and privileges of the abolished Parishads were vested in the Government. Article 59 of the Constitution provides that local government in any administrative unit of the Republic shall be entrusted to bodies composed of persons elected in accordance with law. It was challenged as a colourable legislation because by vesting the rights, powers, authorities and privileges of the abolished parishads in the government, indirectly local government functions of the Upazila Parishad were sought to be entrusted to persons who were not elected by the people, result being that in form it is a Repeal Act, but in substance it continued the Upazila Parishads and vested the rights, powers, authorities and privileges of the Parishads in the Government. Article 59 requires that the Upazila Parishad shall be composed of elected persons and Article 60 requires the Parliament to confer necessary powers including the power to impose taxes for local purposes upon the local bodies, but the Repeal Act, in the guise of abolition of the Parishads, has, in fact, retained them so that their functions can be performed by government through their officers. Their Lordships held that "if this contention is correct and the Upazila Parishads are still functioning through government officers, then the Act will not only be colourable legislation, but it will be a fraud on the Constitution, in which case we shall have no hesitation to declare it void." 

 In Modern Constitutions State powers are distributed among the three Organs or Departments of Government. Legislature is one of the three organs. It is assigned the legislative powers which are clearly demarcated and it has to act within its own field and cannot transgress the limits set by the Constitutional provisions. If the Legislature transgresses the limits, it may be stopped and the transgression may be declared a nullity by the Judiciary—another State Organ. The transgression may be "patent, manifest or direct"; it may also be "disguised, covert and indirect". This latter class of transgression is expressed as colourable legislation in judicial pronouncements. Elaborating this doctrine Duff-J made the following observation in Attorney-General for Ontario vs Reciprocal Insurers, 1924 AC 328; 

 23. The appeal in Kudrat-e-Elahi's case was however dismissed on the technical ground that Article 9 postulating promotion of local government institutions and falling under the Fundamental Principles of State Policy cannot be judicially enforceable and the Upazila Parishad was not a local body. In that case Shahabuddin Ahmed, CJ observed; "It appears to us that the words rights, powers, authorities and privileges of the abolished Parishad have apparently created an impression that those attributes of the Parishad have remained to be enjoyed by the Government, If these words are deleted then no confusion is left". Mr Mahmudul Islam in his Constitutional Law of Bangladesh observed at page 306 (4.29) that when legislature uses certain words in the law, the question of deletion of those words is a matter for consideration of the legislature and not of the court. If those words create unconstitutionality, the words should be declared ultra vires, provided those words are severable, otherwise the whole law is to be declared ultra vires. 

 37. Now that "Certificate", according to Black and P Rahmanatha" being a written testimony to the truth of any fact "and according to Article 81(3) of the Constitution every money Bill shall, when it is presented to the President for his assent, bear as certificate under the hand of the Speaker "that" it is a "Money Bill" convey in the clearest of term that before such a certificate is issued the Speaker must "satisfy" himself that what he is certifying is a money Bill and a Money Bill alone, reason being two-fold firstly, this is a constitutional power granted to him by the people to be exercised on behalf of the people and shall be effected only under, and by authority of the Constitution (Article 7(1) of the Constitution) and secondly, because the grant of power under Article 81(3) of the Constitution itself has placed a condition or an embargo upon such power by employing the expression "that" the Bill shall bear a certificate under the hand of the Speaker "that" it is a Money Bill. As such, it is not an open-handed licence rather the power to exercise this grant of power is qualified and hedged with a condition which of necessity is required to be fulfilled as a condition precedent before the power can be exercised. It is so, because this extraordinary power is granted to the Speaker only as a means of ''shortening the process" of passing a Bill without the rigours of discussion in the parliamentary standing committee and the first, second and third reading of the Bill in the House of Parliament and this is necessary because on occasions the Government may need to raise money immediately by way of imposition of tax or levy -or by borrowing and the normal and usual practice may frustrate the very purpose. Furthermore, by this exercise of power by the Speaker, the President is denied, denuded and robbed of his constitutional prerogative granted to him under Article 80(3) of the Constitution. This is permissible only when the concerned Bill is a Money Bill and Money Bill alone. The Speaker's certificate is not at all necessary if the Bill is not a Money Bill according to Article 81(1) of the Constitution. If the Bill is other than a Money Bill the President under sub-Article (3) of Article 80 of the Constitution may return it to Parliament with a message requesting that the Bill or any particular provisions thereof be reconsidered, and that any amendments specified by him in the message be considered. Under sub-Article 4 of Article 80 as aforesaid if the Bill is so returned the Parliament shall consider the same together with the President's message and if the Bill is again passed by Parliament with or without amendments [by the votes of a majority of the total number of members of Parliament] as pointed out by Mr Abdur Razzaq, learned Counsel appearing in Writ Petition No. 4430 of 2000. He argued that once such a Bill is returned by the President under Article 80(3) of the Constitution, the Parliament though may pass the Bill again with or without amendments shall have to consider it together with the President's message and this requirement is not an idle exercise inasmuch as sub-Article (4) of Article 80 of the Constitution enjoins that if the President so returns the Bill, Parliament shall consider it together with the President's message (emphasis is mine) and such a Bill can be passed by Parliament (with or without amendments) by the votes of a majority of the total number of members of Parliament. Normally a Bill may be passed by the vote of the majority of members present. But according to sub-Article (2) of Article 75 of the Constitution, only 60 (sixty) members do form a quorum. Therefore, a Bill may be passed by a majority of those sixty members present. Whereas, if a Bill is returned to the Parliament for reconsideration (when it is a Bill other than a Money Bill as is the case before us) it can only be passed by the votes of a majority of the total number of members of Parliament as provided under Article 80(4) of the Constitution and Rule 98 of the Rules of Procedure meaning thereby that of the 330 members a minimum of 166 members are required to pass a Bill returned by the President. A money Bill as we have seen under Article 80(3) of the Constitution that the President has no power to return to the Parliament for reconsideration. 

 Article 102 does not specially grant any power of judicial review of legislation on the ground of contravention of the provisions of the Constitution other than the provisions of Part III of the Constitution. However, judicial review of laws is implicit in any written Constitution providing for a limited government, that is, a government in which powers of all functionaries are limited and HC-78 circumscribed by the Constitution, and absence of express power of judicial review is of no consequence. When Article 102 is read with Article 7 there is no difficulty in finding the power of the Supreme Court to declare void any provision of law on the ground of inconsistency with any provision of the Constitution and the Supreme Court has been exercising that power in applications filed under Article 102. Kudrat-e-Elahi vs Bangladesh, 44 DLR (AD) 319. 

 51. In the case of Asma Mani vs Government of Pakistan PLD 1972 SC 139 Hamoodur Rahman CJ, held "I am, therefore unable to agree with the learned Attorney-General that this Presidential order could have amended the Constitution and taken away, as it has purported to do, the jurisdiction of the High Courts to even receive or entertain any complaint, petition, application or other representation whatsoever against, or in relation to the exercise of any power or jurisdiction by any special Military court or Summary Military court or any Martial Law Authority or any person exercising power or jurisdiction derived from the Martial Law Authority under Article 98 of the Constitution of 1962 (equivalent to Article 102 of Bangladesh Constitution), which had been preserved even by the Provisional Constitutional Order of 1969, 

 52. This provision, as very appropriately pointed out by Mr Brohi, strikes at the very root of the judicial power of the court to hear and determine a matter, even though it may relate to its own jurisdiction. The courts undoubtedly have the power to hear and determine any matter or controversy which is brought before them, even if it be to decide whether they have the jurisdiction to determine such a matter or not. The Superior Courts are, as is now well settled, the Judges of their own jurisdiction. This is a right which has been consistently claimed by this and other courts of superior jurisdiction in all civilised countries and it is on the basis of this very right that this court itself went into the question of the validity of the Martial Law in Dosso's case. If Muhammad Munir CJ in 1958 could feel that the courts "on being properly moved still had the right to say whether what had happened was legal or illegal" then what has happened since to take away the right, what was done in 1958 can still be done even though the result might well be different. In that case the learned Attorney-General of Pakistan like Mr Mahmudul Islam the Attorney-General of Bangladesh argued that where there is a written constitution, the courts are themselves creations of the Constitution and have only such jurisdiction as the Constitution chooses to confer upon them to which Hamoodur Rahman CJ, said "I have no cavil with this proposition, as I have myself in several cases indicated, that the Constitution can confer or to restrict the jurisdiction of even superior courts but this is not the same thing as saying that it can also restrict or curtail the judicial power, because, that, in effect, would be denying to the court the very function for which it exists i.e. to decide a controversy even if it relates to its own jurisdiction." 

 53. In the case of Fazlul Quader Chowdhury vs Muhammad Abdul Haque 18 DLR (SC) 69 their Lordships held that the consistent rule of construction adopted by all courts is that provision seeking to oust the jurisdiction of the superior -courts are to be construed strictly with a pronounced leaning against ouster and that it is no doubt true that the courts are not above the Constitution and the source of their jurisdiction as well as its Constitution itself, I do not seek to claim for the courts any higher jurisdiction, but I would venture to point out that it is the cardinal principle that in every system of government operating under a written Constitution the function of finally determining its meaning must be located in some body of authority and the organ of Government which is normally considered most competent to exercise this function is the judiciary. 

 "The judiciary or judicial department is an independent and equal coordinate branch of Government, and is that branch thereof which is intended to interpret, construe, and apply the law, or that department of Government which is charged with the declaration of what the law is, and its construction, so far as it is written law. 

 "In exercising this power, the judiciary claims no supremacy over other organs of the Government but acts only as the administrator of the public will. Even when it declares a legislative measure unconstitutional and void, it does not do so, because, the judicial power is superior in degree or dignity to the legislative power, but because the Constitution has vested it with the power to declare what the law is in the cases which come before it. It thus merely enforces the Constitution as a paramount law whenever a legislative enactment comes into conflict with it because; it is its duty to see that the Constitution prevails. It is only when the Legislature fails to keep within its own Constitutional limits; the judiciary steps in to enforce compliance with the Constitution. This is, no doubt, a delicate task as pointed out in the case of AK Fazlul Quader Chowdhury vs Shah Nawaz, which has to be performed with great circumspection but it has nevertheless to be performed as a sacred Constitutional duty when other State functionaries disregard the limitations imposed upon them or claim to exercise power which the people have been careful to withhold from them. 

 67. Thus it appears that the existing Penal laws are not adequate to control/check some serious and grave offences such as hijacking, collection of subscription, etc. and that under no law in vogue in the country those offences have been properly defined thus creating complication in the conduct of those cases and, as such, the accused apprehended /arrested for committing serious offences get acquitted/released through the loopholes of law. Now, if we look for example at section 10 of the PSA it becomes apparently clear that several offences under the Penal Code such as sections 435/430/141-151 have been jumbled up together and in the name of properly defining the offences section 10 has been rendered incapable of understanding even for a legal wizard. Hence without any doubt it suffers from vagueness and it suffers from lack of guideline because for example in Writ Petition No. 76 of 2001 on the same facts the same police officer recorded two cases; one under sections 143/448/323/427/380 of the Penal Code and the other one under section 10 of the PSA both bearing Khulshi PS Case No. 15 dated 26-12-2000 vide annexures "X" and "Y" to the Supplementary affidavit of the petitioner and this is not denied by the respondent Government, Rather in their affidavit-in-opposition they (respondents) had admitted it at paragraph 7 and stated that the delinquent officer as a measure of punishment had been placed under suspension. It is further stated that the officer noted the Penal Code sections without realising the gravity of the offence and as soon as he realised it, he had the error corrected by inserting section 10 of the PSA although at the time of hearing of the case Mr Mahbubey Alam, learned Additional Attorney-General, in arguing the case (as the learned Attorney-General felt embarrassed to conduct this particular case) admitted that in the facts and circumstances of the case section 10 is not attracted. The case at best attracted section 7 of the PSA which is equivalent to section 427 of the Penal Code i.e. mischief, Mention may be made here that the affidavit-in-opposition has been sworn in by one Md Rafiquzzaman a Senior Assistant Secretary of the Ministry of Home Affairs affirming that since "I deal with the records relevant to this case and, as such, (sic) I am fully conversant with the facts and circumstances of the case and competent therefore to swear this affidavit-in-opposition." Abdul Matin, Sub-Inspector of Police Khulshi Police Station, Chittagong who recorded the first information report has been imp leaded as respondent No. 4 but he did not contest the case by filing any affidavit-in-opposition though he is the only competent person to say why and under what circumstance he filed two first information reports under two different laws. And if he as maintained by the learned Additional Attorney-General was wrong in noting the case initially under the Penal Code and for this fault and negligence was dealt with by being placed under suspension why it was argued that the case did not attract section 10 to which it was changed and that at best it attracted section 7 of the PSA corresponding to section 427 of the Penal Code (mischief). 

 70. If the legislature undertakes to define by statute a new offence and to provide for its punishment, it should express its will in language that will not deceive the common mind, every man being entitled to know that certainty when he has committed a crime. In support of this contention Dr Kamal Hossain referred to a case from the American jurisdiction i.e. 92 US 214 United States vs Reese ET Al. In that case the Supreme Court held that "it would be dangerous if the legislature could set a net large enough to catch all possible offenders, and leave it to the courts to step inside and say who could be rightfully detained, and who should be set at large. This would, to some extent, substitute the judicial for the legislative department of the government. The Courts enforce the legislative will when ascertained, if within the constitutional grant of power. Within its legitimate sphere, congress is supreme, and beyond the control of the courts; but if it steps outside of its Constitutional limitations, and attempts that which is beyond its reach, the courts are authorised to, and when called upon in due course of legal proceedings, must, annul its encroachments upon the reserved power of the States and the People." 

 "The position of the preamble of the Constitution of Bangladesh is somewhat different and it should not be, it is submitted, likened to the preamble of a statute. The preamble is a part of our Constitution and cannot be amended without a referendum. The framers of the Constitution took pains to state clearly the philosophy, aims and objectives of the Constitution and to describe the qualitative aspects of the polity the Constitution is designed to achieve. In this situation, the preamble of the Constitution, in its role, cannot be relegated to the position of the preamble of a statute. However, clear a provision of the Constitution may be, if it is found that the plain meaning of the provision runs counter to the spirit and objectives of the Constitution as stated in the preamble, the question should immediately be asked whether the framers of the Constitution intended to bring about the result which the literal construction produces and the court should search for a meaning in conformity with the spirit and objectives of the Constitution as indicated in the preamble because the substantive provisions have been made to achieve the objects and purposes stated in the preamble. It does not, however, mean that the court can stretch the meaning of the preamble so as to receive support for an interpretation the court wants to give. In Registrar, University of Dacca vs Sajjad Hussain 34 DLR (AD) 1 the majority judgment of the Appellate Division referred to the "historic struggle for national liberation' mentioned in the preamble and construed it as being one phase of the continuing struggle after liberation and for such a construction analogy was drawn from communist political philosophy. It is submitted that the qualifying words 'for national liberation' restricted the expanse of the 'historic struggle' which ended with national independence and cannot be comprehended as continuing after the achievement of independence. Furthermore, the Constitution of Bangladesh clearly envisages traditional democratic process and its language cannot be construed with reference to a radically different political philosophy merely because of the use of the words 'socialist society' in the preamble. This brings us to the expression 'socialism' and 'socialist society' used in the preamble. Apparently, these expressions are vague, but the vagueness disappears when we pay attention to the fact that the framers not only used these expressions but also stated the mode of achieving it by using the expression 'through democratic process' and providing in the substantive part of the Constitution a 18th Century tripartite form of government. Read in the proper perspective, there remains no doubt that the framers did not allude to the communist philosophy of State organisation, but conceived of a democratically-run welfare State to eliminate inequality of income and status and standards of life, and to provide a decent standard of living to the working mass of the country. The preamble speaks of 'equality and justice, political, economic and social.' This brings in the concept of distributive justice which aims at removal of economic inequalities and the undoing of injustice resulting from transactions and dealings between unequal’s in the society. This becomes further clear if we refer to Articles. 14 and 19 of the Constitution. The preamble also speaks of the supremacy of the Constitution, rule of law and fundamental human right which will be dealt with separately". 

 And Whereas investigations conducted by the Government through its agencies have also disclosed similar offences committed during the period aforesaid; 

 2. The Central Government shall by notification create adequate number of courts to be called Special Courts. 

 4. (1) If the Central Government is of the opinion that there is prima facie evidence of the commission of an offence alleged to have been committed during the period mentioned in the preamble by a person who held high public or political office in India and that in accordance with the guidelines contained in the preamble hereto said offence ought to be dealt with under the Act, the Central Government shall make a declaration to that effect in every case in which it is of the aforesaid opinion. (2) such declaration shall not be called in question in any court. 

 5. On such declaration being made any prosecution in respect of such offence shall be instituted only in a Special Court designated by the Central Government and any prosecution in respect of such offence pending in any court in India shall stand transferred to a Special Court designated by the Central Government. 

 7. A Special Court shall be presided over by a sitting Judge of a High Court in India or a person who has held office as a Judge of a High Court in India and nominated by the Central Government in consultation with the Chief Justice of India. 

 "that the provisions of the Bill and the recitals of the preamble provide sufficient and definite guidance for making the requisite declaration for deciding who should be sent up for trial to the Special Courts; that, in the context, the Bill does not vest arbitrary or uncanalised power in the Government to pick and choose persons for being tried by special Courts; that the procedure prescribed by the Bill for trial before the Special Courts, far from being more onerous than the ordinary procedure, is in certain important respects more beneficial to the accused; and since, in any event, the procedure of the Special Courts is not more onerous than the ordinary procedure, the provisions of the Bill involve no discrimination violative of Article 14. 

 74. Sufficient guideline was provided in the preamble of the reported case unlike the PSA, Besides that, though there is a provision for making rule under section 25 of the PSA but no such rules have, for reasons known to the Government, been framed till date. 

 4(1) ''If the central government is of the 'opinion that there is prima facie evidence of the commission of an offence alleged to have been committed during the period mentioned in the preamble by a person who held high public or political office in India and that in accordance with the guidelines contained in the preamble hereto the said offence ought to be dealt with under the Act, the central Government shall make a declaration to that effect in every case in which it is of the aforesaid opinion." 

 77. In our own jurisdiction we do have an appropriate case where the law was declared ultra vires and void for lack of guidelines. On a reading of the PSA, it is abundantly clear that it allows the police an arbitrary and unguided discretion to apply the law and on this ground it is unconstitutional and void being discriminatory and violative of the equality provision of the Constitution. Dr Kamal Hossain, Mr Syed Ishtiaq Ahmed and Mr Abdur Razzaque relied on the case of Dr Nurul Islam vs Bangladesh 33 DLR (AD) 201 in which case their Lordships held "after having considered the arguments of the learned Counsel and the cases cited by him in support of his contentions that section 9(2) of the Public Servants Retirement Act, 1974 providing for compulsory retirement of public servants completing 25 years of service was challenged on the ground that the law, conferring discretion on the government to retire a public servant without providing any guideline, was violative of Articles 27 and 29 of the Constitution upon consideration of a large number of decisions including Jibendra Kishore, East and West Steamship Co. Waris Meah, Munim J (with whom Ruhul Islam and BH Chowdhury JJ agreed) observed: 

 "The minimum principle or guideline as has been provided in service rules as appeared from the cases in this judgment is that of the public servant or the interest of public service. In either the impugned Act or the rules made thereunder provided such principle, the minimum requirement of law as showing the existence of some guideline for the exercise of discretion in retiring a Government servant who has completed 25 years of service would, I think, be satisfied, thus making it immune from any challenge on the ground of discrimination violative of Articles 27 and 29 of the Constitution. I am of opinion therefore, that in the absence of such a guideline either in the Act or the rules framed thereunder, section 9(2) suffers from unconstitutionality. Dr Nurul Islam and 3 others were retired under section 9(2) as they completed 25 years of service although there were 31 others who had also completed 25 years of service. Dr Nurul Islam was replaced by Dr Maniruzzaman who was senior to Dr Islam both in age and service by three years. This could be done because there was no guideline as to how the selection for compulsory retirement would be made. Previously there was a guideline namely "in the public interest." This was omitted and was not in place when Dr Islam was retired. After Dr Nurul Islam successfully challenged his retirement the guideline of public interest was once again inserted by way of amendment and the decision in Mafizur Rahman's case 34 DLR (AD) 321 was different. On the right to equality Mr Mahmudul Islam in his Constitutional Law of Bangladesh said. 

 "The principle enunciated by the Indian Supreme Court that a law will not be held discriminatory when unguided discretion is given to a high and responsible officer on the expectation that the discretion will he exercised reasonably is difficult to accept. The expression 'reasonable' is vacuous unless used with reference to a specific standard and in the absence of a standard no exercise of discretion can be judged for reasonableness. Furthermore, in our society we have found high and responsible officers acting arbitrarily even though such arbitrariness is hard to prove in the absence of any standard of reasonableness, particularly in the face of presumption of legality of official acts. In Dr Nurul Islam's case the government urged the principle, but the Appellate Division rightly did not accept the principle even though the discretion was conferred on the government itself." 

 "Contemporaneous law and retrospectively: Article 31 guarantees that an individual shall be dealt with in accordance with law. Thus an individual cannot be prejudicially affected unless there is contemporaneously in existence a legal provision to sustain the action. A person shall not be prevented from or hindered in doing an act which is not prohibited by law. A public functionary in discharge of his official function taking away a car of an individual without any authority of law, the action is not only illegal, but also violative of the fundamental right guaranteed under Article 31. The question is, whether Parliament can retrospectively validate an act which was unconstitutional because of the absence of any contemporaneous law to sustain the act. The Appellate Division in Mofizur Rahman vs Bangladesh answered the question in the affirmative. The provision of section 9(2) of the Public Servants Retirement Act, 1974 conferring a discretion on the government to retire public servants on completion of 25 years of service was declared void by the Appellate Division as being discriminatory for want of any guideline for the exercise of the discretion. As a result, all actions under the Act retiring public servants became unconstitutional. Section 9(2) was later amended providing the guideline of 'public interest' and the amending Act validated the previous actions retiring public servants. The court referred to a number of decisions of the Indian Supreme Court, the British Indian Federal Court and the Australian High Court and took note of the difference in language between Article 31 and Article 35 to hold that the expression "in accordance with law" does not mean "in accordance with law in force" at the time of taking action and upheld the amending Act validating the unconstitutional actions of retirement of public servants. It is submitted that reference to the decisions of the Indian Supreme Court is inappropriate inasmuch as the Indian Constitution does not contain any provision similar to Article 31. The same was the position under the Government of India Act, 1935 and in the Australian jurisdiction. A noted author criticised the Indian Supreme Court for not considering whether those validating laws were reasonable restrictions within the meaning of Article 19 of the Indian Constitution and made a comparative study of the British, Canadian, Australian and Indian positions. The absence of the expression 'in force at the time of commission of the act' may be important in determining the permissibility of retrospective laws. The difference in language is there because the framers of the Constitution did not intend to take away the power of Parliament to enact retrospective laws which do not offend the constitutional limitation, but from the said difference of language an interpretation cannot be given to permit Parliament to avoid the constitutional limitation of Article 31 or render Article 31 nugatory. In the American jurisdiction, the legislature has the power to pass retrospective laws if the retrospectively does not offend any provision of the constitution including the 'due process' clause. When a law is passed, the retrospective aspect of the legislation, as well as the prospective aspects, must meet the test of due process and the justifications for the latter may not suffice for the former. Even when the court finds the law (operating prospectively) valid under the due process clause, the court will have the further duty to inquire whether the retrospective operation given to the law is unreasonable or arbitrary, or, in other words, the court will inquire whether there was a rational relationship between the retrospectively and the legitimate governmental interest sought to be achieved by the retrospectively. When a retrospective law is once covered by Article 35 no question of reasonableness will arise, and the very fact that the law is retrospective will be sufficient for the court to declare it void. The question of reasonableness will be moot when such law is not covered by Article 35. Parliament has power to make retrospective laws; the only limitation is that like all other laws it must pass the test of constitutionality under Article 31 and the retrospectively must not be arbitrary or unreasonable. If the retrospectively is found to be arbitrary or unreasonable, it will be violative of Article 31 and therefore void."

In the case of Saleha Khatun vs Administrative Tribunal 3 BLC (AD) 158 their Lordships held: 

 "The preamble of the Constitution of Bangladesh states 'rule of law' as one of the objectives to be attained. The expression "rule of law" has various shades of meaning and it is an ever expanding concept. AV Dicey's concept of rule of law included three things—(i) absence of arbitrary power, that is, no man is above law and the persons in authority do not enjoy wide, arbitrary or discretionary powers, (ii) equality before law, and jurisdiction of ordinary courts, and (iii) individual liberties. His thesis has been criticised from many angles, but his emphasis on subjection of every person to the ordinary laws of the land, the absence of arbitrary power and legal protection for certain basic human rights remains the undisputed theme of the doctrine of rule of law. According to Professor Wade rule of law connotes three ideas—(1) it expresses a preference for law and order within a community rather than anarchy, warfare and constant strife, (2) it expresses a legal doctrine of fundamental importance, namely, that government must be conducted according to law, and that in disputed cases what the law requires is declared by judicial decisions and (3) it refers to a body of political opinion about what the declared rules on law should provide in matters both of substance and of procedure. The first two ideas are not sufficient in achieving a democratic society in which human dignity and freedom may be ensured, for, in a dictatorship, law and order can be maintained and the government can be run in accordance with law promulgated by the dictator and yet there may not be any freedom of the people if the law make by the dictator does not provide for such freedom. For this the third idea is added to make the concept a meaningful one. "Law in the context of the rule of law does not mean any law enacted by the legislative authorities, however arbitrary or despotic it may be what is necessary element of the rule of law it that law must not be arbitrary or irrational and it must satisfy the test of reason and the democratic form of the polity seeks to ensure this element by making the framer of the law accountable to the people," The concept is now intended to imply not only that (1) the powers exercised by State functionaries must have a legal basis, that is, they must be based on authority conferred by law, but also that (ii) the law should conform to certain minimum standards of justice, both substantive and procedural." The concept implies that the ruler must also be subject to law. It is the subordination of all authorities, legislative, executive and others to certain principles which would generally be accepted as characteristic of law, such as the ideas of the fundamental principles of justice, normal principles, fairness and due process. It implies respect for the supreme value and dignity of the individual. "It is generally agreed that the minimum content of the concept is that "the law affecting individual liberty ought to be reasonably certain or predictable; where the law confers wide discretionary powers there should be adequate safeguards against their abuse; like should be treated alike, and unfair discrimination must not be sanctioned by law; a person ought not to be deprived of his liberty, status or any other substantial interest unless he is given the opportunity of a fair hearing before an impartial tribunal; and so forth. "The rule of law demands that power is to be exercised in a manner which is just, fair and reasonable and not in an unreasonable, capricious or arbitrary manner leaving room for discrimination. It requires that decisions should be made by the application of known principles and rules and in general, such decisions should be predictable and the citizen should know where he stands; a decision without any principle or rule is unpredictable and is the antithesis of a decision in accordance with the rule of law.
